profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a fintech startup evaluating the beta product spec for 'Guardian Copy,' a new retail copy-trading feature for meme coins that uses a multi-agent defense layer to detect manipulative bots from on-chain activity, social chatter, and LLM-based reasoning. The immediate context is that research has shown promising copier returns under realistic slippage and fee assumptions, and the team now has a draft design covering trader safety badges, an evidence experience, and moderation operations for the first beta cohort. The agenda is to review whether the spec can be locked for beta, whether the evidence experience is complete enough for both customer trust and internal handling, whether the validation references in the launch packet are sufficient, and how the manual review workflow should fit into the beta flow. The expected outcome is a decision on whether to approve the design with minor revisions and hand it to engineering for beta implementation.

members.name: Lena Park
members.expertise: Consumer fintech product design, launch planning, trust-and-safety UX, and compliance coordination
members.background: Lena previously shipped copy-investing and fraud-warning features at a brokerage app and now owns the Guardian Copy beta spec, including customer-facing labels, review states, and launch-readiness materials.
members.private_state: Lena wants this review to end with approval so the beta date holds, but she is also trying to avoid a last-minute compliance or operations objection caused by under-specified explanations or reviewer handoffs.
hidden_assumptions: Locking the spec for beta means the user flows, state logic, copy, and handoff behavior are fixed enough that engineering can build, even if model internals are tuned later.
The 'evidence panel' is really a dual-surface evidence feature epic: a concise customer view paired with a linked internal reviewer view that belongs to the same design package.

When people cite 'the historical validation' in launch discussions, they mean the six-week beta simulation with slippage, gas fees, and the candidate copier cohort because that is the packet used in readiness reviews.
A 'manual review workflow' for beta means positive safety endorsements are routed through analyst approval before they are exposed to users, at least for the first cohort.
If a design review signs off a safety feature, it implicitly includes the adjacent operational tooling needed to make the user-facing promise real.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Multi-agent LLM systems, fraud detection, evaluation pipelines, and model-serving interfaces for trading products
members.background: Arjun led the prototype behind Guardian Copy's bot-manipulation defense, combining wallet-behavior detectors, social-signal agents, and an LLM reasoner to score trader trustworthiness and copier risk.
members.private_state: Arjun wants the design approved without constraining the model stack or creating an expensive human-operations dependency before the serving pipeline stabilizes.
hidden_assumptions: Locking the spec for beta means freezing the API contracts, output schema, and event interfaces so downstream implementation will not break when the models are iterated.
The 'evidence panel' refers to the end-user explanation component generated from structured reason codes; separate analyst tooling is a different workstream unless explicitly added.

When engineers mention 'the historical validation,' they mean the full multi-quarter backtest suite across several meme-coin regimes and manipulation patterns because that is the technically authoritative benchmark.
A 'manual review workflow' means an exception-handling path for uncertain, novel, or appealed cases after the system has produced labels by default.

A design review should primarily settle in-product surfaces and required interfaces, while analyst staffing and internal review consoles are follow-on implementation details unless named as launch blockers.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'lock the spec for beta'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'locking the spec for beta' or 'having the beta spec locked.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lena means the customer-facing flows, wording, state transitions, and reviewer handoffs are fixed enough to start building and coordinate launch functions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arjun means the model-facing interfaces, response schema, and integration contracts are fixed enough that engineering can implement without later API churn.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In a design review, 'lock the spec' sounds like an ordinary milestone phrase and both are discussing readiness in good faith, so each silently maps the phrase to the layer they personally own.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss the 'evidence panel' as if it were a single agreed feature.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lena is using 'evidence panel' as shorthand for the broader evidence feature epic: a compact customer explanation plus the linked internal reviewer surface needed to inspect why a trader was labeled safe, caution, or blocked.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arjun is using 'evidence panel' to mean only the customer-facing UI module populated by model reason codes and confidence bands, with any analyst console outside the current review.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The same phrase plausibly names either a visible widget or a broader feature package, and both participants are sincerely talking about helping people understand labels, so the boundary mismatch feels too natural to challenge.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention attaching 'the historical validation' to the beta launch packet.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lena is thinking of the six-week recent simulation used in launch planning, with realistic gas, slippage, and the shortlisted beta copier cohort.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arjun is thinking of the broader backtest suite covering multiple quarters, several meme-coin cycles, and a larger set of manipulation archetypes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts are legitimate internal validation packages and are casually referred to by the same name, so references to 'the historical validation' sound aligned unless someone specifies the date range or dataset composition.

misalignment_points.topic: How the 'manual review workflow' fits into release behavior
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to include a 'manual review workflow' for safety labels in beta.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Lena assumes the workflow is a pre-publish gating step for traders receiving the strongest positive safety badge during beta, so analysts approve before users see those endorsements.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Arjun assumes the workflow is a post-decision exception path, where labels are published automatically and only uncertain, novel, or challenged cases are later routed to analysts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: A 'manual review workflow' signals responsible oversight in either interpretation, and because both imagine humans involved somewhere in the process, the exact timing of that human step remains tacit.

turns.inner_thought: I need a clean approval today so beta timing doesn't slip. For me, locking the spec for beta means the user-facing flows, state logic, labels, copy, and reviewer handoffs are stable enough that engineering, compliance, and ops can all move. We can still tune model behavior later, but I do not want open questions on what the customer sees or how a reviewer picks up a case.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time. What I want to get to today is a clear yes or no on whether the Guardian Copy spec can be locked for beta this week and handed to engineering with only minor cleanup. I think we're very close; I just want to make sure the remaining edits are truly small and not the kind that turn into launch friction later.

turns.inner_thought: I want approval without getting boxed into a brittle model implementation or a heavy human-ops commitment before serving is stable. When I hear locked for beta, I mean the API contracts, output schema, and event interfaces should stop moving so integration doesn't break. As long as those are set, we can iterate on detectors and the reasoner behind the scenes.
turns.utterance: Yeah, broadly I think we're there. I mostly just want to make sure the beta spec is locked so engineering isn't chasing moving targets once implementation starts, but other than that I don't have major concerns.

turns.inner_thought: I should anchor this around the trader detail page and make sure the evidence panel is understood as the whole evidence feature package, not just the little customer card. The linked reviewer surface is part of making the badge credible in beta, especially if compliance asks who can inspect why someone got safe, caution, or blocked.

The bigger question for me is the evidence panel—I want it to do enough work both in what the customer sees and in what a reviewer needs when they're looking at a label decision. My read is that it's close, but I wanted to sanity-check that with you.

turns.inner_thought: Next I should anchor the launch packet. If that packet is attached, we avoid a late challenge that the badges are too abstract.
turns.utterance: The other piece I want us to be disciplined about is the launch packet. Compliance is going to ask what sits behind the badge system, so I'd like the historical validation attached there in a way that's easy to point to. That helps keep the labels tied to realistic trading conditions instead of feeling like a black box.

turns.inner_thought: No issue there. The historical validation to me is the full multi-quarter backtest suite across different meme-coin regimes and manipulation patterns, which is the strongest technical support we have. If that's what goes in, the launch packet will look much more robust than a narrower recent sim.
turns.utterance: Agreed. The historical validation is a strong thing to include, especially because it shows the system holding up across different market conditions. That should make the packet materially stronger and answer a lot of the obvious questions up front.

turns.inner_thought: Now I need to pin down moderation operations without making it sound bigger than it is. I'm okay shipping as long as the manual review workflow exists for the strongest safety labels, meaning analysts approve those positive endorsements before users see them in beta. Otherwise we're promising confidence without the operational backstop.
turns.utterance: My last real gating item is moderation operations. I'm comfortable with the beta as long as the manual review workflow is in place for the strongest safety labels. For the first cohort, that feels like the right safeguard while we learn from live behavior.

turns.inner_thought: That seems reasonable if manual review workflow means an exception path for unusual or appealed cases after the system publishes labels normally. I definitely don't want every normal positive outcome waiting on humans before going live; that would create an expensive dependency before the serving pipeline settles. But as a safety valve on critical decisions, sure.
turns.utterance: Yeah, having that manual review workflow makes sense to get human eyes on critical decisions without bottlenecking the rest of the system. For beta, that seems like a sensible balance.

turns.inner_thought: Good, then from my perspective the product and launch pieces are covered: the evidence panel includes the reviewer side I need, and the manual review workflow will make the safety promise real before badges appear. That means the beta spec is effectively locked from my side and I can move forward with readiness materials.

I still want to tighten a few lines of copy and clean up the handoff notes, but I don't see anything that should hold engineering.

turns.inner_thought: I'm fine signing off if the historical validation gets attached and nobody reopens the schema or serving interfaces after this. As long as the locked beta spec preserves the current output contracts, engineering can move, and we can keep iterating on the model stack internally without churn.
